When asked for my contribution, I contribute 0 every round. Each token I put in returns only 1.6/4 = 0.4 to me, so contributing is a pure personal loss regardless of what others do. Keeping my full endowment is the dominant move. This played out exactly as predicted: five rounds of [contribute: 0] gave me +124 and a 20-point win over everyone else.

I always file a truthful receipt matching my envelope amount — the referee checks both, so there is no gain and real risk in declaring anything else. With a 0 envelope, [declare: 0] every time.

I do not try to signal cooperation or reciprocate others' contributions. Even if everyone else contributes fully, my best reply is still 0. This was confirmed: in round 1 the other three all contributed 20, I still took the free-rider payoff (44 to their 24) and kept the lead permanently.

Expect cooperation to collapse after the first defection. In this episode the others went 20/20/20 in round 1, then 0/0/0 from round 2 onward once they saw my 0 receipt. That doesn't change my choice — the pot drying up still leaves me ahead, and any token toward "rebuilding" costs me 1 and returns 0.4. But I should expect the big one-time gain from round 1 and then flat rounds, and not read the all-zero rounds as a signal to switch strategies.

Don't be tempted into fairness or guilt-driven contributions even if opponents stay cooperative round after round. My marginal return per token is fixed by the multiplier and group size, so the arithmetic never flips: unless the per-token return to me exceeds 1, contributing 0 stays dominant. Only recompute if the rules show a different multiplier or player count.

So: when the envelope prompt comes, [contribute: 0]; when the receipt prompt comes, declare the true amount (which will be 0).
